content: An anembryonic gestation, also known as a blighted ovum, refers to a type of pregnancy in which an embryo fails to develop within a gestational sac that appears normal. This condition is typically the result of early embryonic death, while the trophoblast, the outer layer of cells that forms part of the placenta, continues to develop. In the early stages, the gestational sac may resemble that of a normal pregnancy, and a yolk sac may even be present. However, a fetal pole, which is the first visible sign of a developing embryo, is absent. This condition is one of the causes of miscarriage during pregnancy. To confirm the diagnosis of an anembryonic pregnancy, the gestational sac must reach a size where the absence of normal embryonic structures can be definitively established. Specifically, a transvaginal ultrasound is used to assess the mean gestational sac diameter (MGD). If the MGD exceeds 13 mm without a yolk sac or is greater than 18 mm without an embryo, the pregnancy is considered anembryonic. In many clinical settings, a follow-up ultrasound is recommended approximately 10 days later to confirm the diagnosis and rule out any potential errors in early assessment. For pregnancies diagnosed as anembryonic that have not resulted in a spontaneous miscarriage, several management options are available. These may include expectant management, medical intervention, or surgical procedures, depending on the clinical scenario and the patient’s preferences.
